entries.title: German at a glance
body: German is a West Germanic language, close to English and Dutch, and the official language of Germany, Austria and much of Switzerland. Nouns are capitalized. The verb in a simple statement sits in second place.
Articles carry the gender: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter). The plural article is die for every gender.

entries.title: Umlauts, ß and ch
body: ä, ö and ü are separate vowels, not decorations. ä is near the vowel in “bed”, ö and ü are rounded (say “ee” with rounded lips for ü). ß is a sharp s, used after a long vowel or diphthong: Fuß, Straße. Switzerland writes ss instead.
ch after a, o, u and au is the sound in Bach. After e, i, ä, ö, ü and the consonants it is softer, as in ich.

head: Spelling
Roughly
rows: like the vowel in French feu
like the vowel in French tu

entries.title: der, die, das in the nominative and accusative
entries.body: Learn each noun with its article. In the accusative (the direct object) only the masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen. die and das stay as they are.

entries.title: The present tense
entries.body: One present covers “I learn” and “I am learning”. Regular verbs add -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. sein and haben are irregular and come up constantly.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: From twenty-one upward, German names the units first: einundzwanzig is “one-and-twenty”. The noun after a number stays singular in the sense that the number itself carries the plural: zwei Bücher, with the noun in the plural form.

entries.title: Please, thanks, and the bill
entries.body: bitte covers both “please” and “you're welcome”. danke is “thank you”. In a café, bitte zahlen or die Rechnung, bitte asks for the bill.

entries.title: Where German is spoken
entries.body: Standard German (Hochdeutsch) is what courses teach. Everyday speech in Bavaria, Austria and Switzerland can sound quite different, and Swiss German is a set of dialects rather than a separate spelling system. Written German is shared, with small differences (ss for ß in Switzerland).
